chunk_findings.detail: `merged()` assumes the "earlier definition" of a self-extending name lives in a strictly lower layer, so it recurses with `merged(name, cands[-2][2], trail)`. When two files in the *same* layer declare the same `name` and the later one has `extends = "<name>"`, `cands[-2][2] == cands[-1][2]`, so `upto` does not decrease and the identical `cands` list is re-derived forever. Concrete input: one layer with `a.toml` (`[doctype] name = "x"`, `path = "a.md"`) and `b.toml` (`[doctype] name = "x"`, `extends = "x"`, plus a path). `resolve` raises `RecursionError` instead of a `DocTypeError`; nothing in `read_raw` rejects the duplicate name, so this is reachable from `registry()`/the `doc types` command.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/services/doctypes/spec.py: resolve()/merged() — self-extend across two defs in the same layer
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/doctypes/spec.py: resolve()/merged() — self-extend across two defs in the same layer

chunk_findings.detail: The pattern is validated with `for p in re.findall(_PLACE, pattern)`, but `_PLACE = r"\{(\w+)(?::[^{}]*)?\}"` only matches `{word}` or `{word:spec}`; any brace group that is not of that shape is simply not seen, so validation passes. `expand()` then calls `pattern.format(...)`. Input `pattern = "docs/{}.md"` (also `"docs/{a-b}.md"`, `"docs/{seq:{w}}.md"`): `build()` returns a valid `DocType(multi=True)`, and `expand()` raises `IndexError` (`KeyError`/`ValueError` for the other two) rather than the descriptor being refused. A validated type is therefore not always expandable, contradicting the "pattern expands deterministically" guarantee.
chunk_findings.location: ddflow/services/doctypes/spec.py: build() placeholder check versus expand()
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/doctypes/spec.py: build() placeholder check versus expand()

chunk_findings.detail: Errors raised for section scalar fields pass no `start` to `_Src.err`, so `_line` searches from line 0 and reports the *first* line in the file matching the key, not the offending section. Input: two sections where the first has `level = 2` and the second has `level = "2"`; the error for the second section points at the first section's line. `_Src.unknown` gets the correct `start`, so only the type/choice violations are mislocated, but every such message names a line that is provably not where the bad value is.

chunk_findings.detail: `_check_pattern` passes the raw value of `pattern` straight into `Formatter().parse(pattern)` (and later `pattern.format(...)`), but `pattern` is read with `raw.get("pattern", "")` and is not type-checked before this call — the `_typed(src, raw, "pattern", str, ...)` check (if present) only runs later, inside the `DocType(...)` construction that `_check_pattern` precedes. Any non-string TOML value reaches `string.Formatter().parse`, which requires a `str` and raises `TypeError` (e.g. "expected str instance, int found"), and `TypeError` is not in the `except (ValueError, KeyError, IndexError)` tuple, so it escapes as an unhandled traceback instead of the promised file:line error. Concrete input: a TOML doctype with `name = "x"`, `multi = true`, `pattern = 5` (or `pattern = ["docs/{slug}.md"]`). `multi` is `True`, the two `multi`/`path` guards fall through (`pattern` is truthy), and `_check_pattern` crashes before the loader can report anything, violating the stated "every error names the file" contract. Adding `TypeError` to the caught tuple (or validating `pattern` with `_typed` before calling `_check_pattern`) makes this input produce the intended `pattern` error.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/doctypes/spec.py:307 (`_check_pattern`)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_merge` assumes a child's `validate`/`review` value is a mapping and splats it: `out[k] = {**parent.get(k, {}), **child[k]}`. If it is not a mapping, this raises a bare `TypeError`, not the promised `DocTypeError` naming the file. Repro: layer 0 `a.toml` = `[doctype]
name="parent"
path="docs/p.md"`, layer 1 `b.toml` = `[doctype]
name="child"
path="docs/c.md"
extends="parent"
review = true`, then `resolve([...])` evaluates `{**{}, **True}` and blows up with `TypeError: 'bool' object is not a mapping`, even though `_review`/`_validate` were written to reject exactly this with `review must be a table` / `validate must be a table`. The non-extends path reaches those clean checks (`build` → `_review`/`_validate`); the extends path crashes before them, so a plausible user typo (`review = true`, `validate = "..."`) yields a traceback instead of a file:line error in `ddflow doc types validate`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/doctypes/spec.py:278-280 (`_merge`)

chunk_findings.detail: Duplicate section ids inside an extending type are silently collapsed instead of refused. `_merge` stores child sections in a dict keyed by `id` and, on a repeated id, does `secs[s["id"]] = {**secs[s["id"]], **s}`, so the last occurrence overwrites the earlier one; `build`/`_sections` (spec.py:314-316) only detect duplicates in the list it receives, which by then has been deduplicated. So a child such as `extends = "parent"` plus two `[[doctype.section]]` blocks both with `id = "intro"` is accepted with data loss (the second wins), whereas the same descriptor without `extends` raises `duplicate section id 'intro'`. The stated requirement "a type with a duplicate section id is refused" therefore holds only for non-extending types; validation should run before the id-keyed merge, or the merge should reject a repeated id.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/doctypes/spec.py:284-292 (`_merge`)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_merge` validates that `child["validate"]` and `child["review"]` are tables, but the very next statement iterates the child's `section` value with `for s in child.get("section", [])` without first checking it is iterable. The per-element guard (`not isinstance(s, dict) or "id" not in s`) only runs *inside* the loop, so a non-iterable value blows up before it can be reached, with a bare `TypeError` rather than the promised `DocTypeError` naming the file. Repro: layer 0 `a.toml` = `[doctype]
name="parent"
path="docs/p.md"`; layer 1 `b.toml` = `[doctype]
name="child"
path="docs/c.md"
extends="parent"
section = 5`; then `resolve([("shipped",[("a.toml",...)]),("project",[("b.toml",...)])])` evaluates `for s in 5` and raises `TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable`, escaping `resolve` uncaught — exactly the failure mode the adjacent guard was added to prevent (the earlier review confirmed merge runs on raw TOML dicts before any schema build, so nothing upstream rejects `section = 5` first). `section = true` fails the same way; only an iterable wrong type (e.g. a string) currently reaches the intended error path.
